items.prompt: Which hook adds a state variable to a function component?

options.label: useEffect
useContext
useRef
useState

rubric: useState declares state in a function component.
useEffect is for side effects, useRef holds mutable references, and useContext reads context.

items.prompt: Which JSX attribute sets the CSS class of an element?

options.label: class
styleClass
cssClass
className

rubric: JSX uses className because class is a reserved word in JavaScript.
class is the HTML attribute name, which learners often carry over.

items.prompt: What is the name of the mechanism used to pass data from a parent component to a child component?

options.label: Effects
Refs
Keys
Props

rubric: Props are the inputs a parent passes to a child.
Refs, keys and effects serve other purposes.

items.prompt: A custom React component's name must start with which kind of character so JSX treats it as a component?

options.label: The word "use"
An underscore
A capital letter
A lowercase letter

rubric: Names starting with a capital letter are treated as components; lowercase names are treated as HTML tags.
"use" is the naming prefix for hooks, not components.

items.prompt: Which JSX syntax embeds the JavaScript variable `name` inside an element's content?

options.label: {{name}}
<name>
${name}
{name}

rubric: Single curly braces embed a JavaScript expression in JSX.
${} is template-literal syntax and double braces are used only for object literals such as style.

items.prompt: Which of the following are built-in React hooks? Select all that apply.

options.label: useRef
useState
useLoop
useFetch
useEffect

rubric: useState, useEffect and useRef ship with React.
useFetch and useLoop are not built in; they would have to be custom hooks.

items.prompt:
A new developer writes a component that returns an `

` followed directly by a `

`, and sees the error "Adjacent JSX elements must be wrapped in an enclosing tag." Which rule should they recall to fix it?

options.label: Wrap both elements in a `<script>` tag inside the return
Turn the component into a class so it can return more than one element
Wrap both in one parent element or a fragment `<>...</>`
Put each element in its own `return` statement, one after another

rubric: A component must return a single root, which can be a parent element or a fragment.
Multiple returns and class conversion do not change this rule.

items.prompt: Why use `useState` for a counter instead of a plain `let count = 0` variable inside the component?

options.label: React only lets you display variables that were declared with useState, so plain ones never show
Changing a plain variable does not trigger a re-render, but setting state does
State values are saved permanently in the browser's storage, so they survive a page reload
Plain variables inside components are constants, so their values can never be changed

rubric: Calling the state setter tells React to re-render with the new value.
Distractors confuse state with persistence or claim variables have type limits.

items.prompt: What does it mean that props are read-only?

options.label: Props are hidden from the child until it asks for them
A child component should not modify the props it receives
A parent component cannot change what it passes to a child
Props can only contain strings and never other values

rubric: Components treat received props as immutable; changes come from the parent passing new values.
Props can hold any value, and parents can pass new ones on later renders.

items.prompt:
Given `function Greeting(props) { return

Hi {props.name}

; }`, what does `` render?

options.label: Hi props.name
Hi {name}
An error, because name is undefined
Hi Ana

rubric: The braces evaluate props.name, which is "Ana".
Other options treat the braces as literal text or assume the prop is missing.

items.prompt: Why does React ask for a `key` prop on items rendered from an array with `map`?

options.label: It helps React track which items were added or removed
It sets the order in which items appear on screen, sorted by key value
It makes each item read-only so it cannot be edited by other components
It passes the item's data to the child as a prop named key

rubric: Keys give list items a stable identity so React can update efficiently.
Key does not control order, immutability, and it is not available as a prop.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between props and state?

options.label: Props are passed in from a parent, while state is owned and updated by the component
Props are saved in the browser between visits, while state is kept on the server for each user
Props can only hold strings and numbers, while state can hold objects and arrays only
Props are changed by the component itself, while state is handed down from its parent

rubric: Props come from outside; state is managed inside the component.
One distractor reverses the roles, the others invent storage or type limits.

items.prompt: Which statements about React components are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: A component must be written as a class to be valid
A component can render other components inside its JSX
A component must create its elements with `document.createElement`
A component can be reused several times with different props

rubric: Reuse with different props and nesting are core ideas of components.
Function components are valid, and JSX removes the need for manual DOM creation.

items.prompt: A learner writes `<button onClick={handleClick()}>Save</button>`. The `handleClick` function runs every time the component renders, not when the button is clicked. Why does this happen?

options.label: React attaches click listeners at render time, so each render triggers the button's click handler once
The parentheses call the function immediately; it should be passed as `handleClick`
JSX needs the lowercase attribute `onclick` for the handler to be deferred until a real click occurs
A handler must be saved in state first, otherwise React runs it during each render to read it

rubric: handleClick() runs while rendering and passes its result; the handler needs the function reference.
Other options blame event naming or state, which are not the cause.

items.prompt: Why should each element in a list rendered with `items.map(...)` get a `key` prop?

options.label: It makes React skip re-rendering the whole list when data changes
It sorts the rendered items so they appear in a stable order
It gives the child component a readable `props.key` value to use
It lets React match each item to the same item between renders

rubric: Keys let React identify which items were added, moved or removed between renders.
Distractors treat the key as a readable prop, a render-skipping tool or a sorting mechanism, which it is not.

items.prompt: In a click handler you call `setCount(count + 1)`. What does React do with that call?

options.label: It reloads the page so the browser shows the updated count value
It schedules a re-render, and the component then runs with the new `count`
It changes `count` at once, so the next line of the handler sees the new value
It updates the real DOM text directly without running the component again

rubric: A state setter schedules a re-render, and the new value is seen in the next render.
Distractors assume state changes immediately like a normal variable or bypasses rendering.

items.prompt: A parent passes `title="Hi"` to a child component. Which statement about that prop is correct?

options.label: The child only receives it after the parent re-renders at least twice
The child may reassign `props.title` to change the text the parent holds
The child must copy it into a global variable before it can read it
The child receives it as read-only data and cannot change the parent's value

rubric: Props flow down from parent to child and are read-only in the child.
Distractors suggest props can be mutated by the child or need special handling.

items.prompt: What is JSX, as used in a React component?

options.label: A template language the browser parses at runtime into real DOM nodes
A string of HTML that React inserts into the page using innerHTML
A separate stylesheet format that React uses to style each component
A syntax extension that is compiled into JavaScript calls creating elements

rubric: JSX is compiled by a build tool into JavaScript function calls that describe elements.
Distractors confuse JSX with browser templates, raw HTML strings or CSS.

items.prompt: In JSX you write `<div className="box">` rather than `<div class="box">`. Why?

options.label: React generates its own class names, so a plain class name is ignored
`class` is a reserved word in JavaScript, and JSX attributes become JS properties
`className` is required by CSS so that styles can be scoped to a component
HTML5 no longer accepts `class`, so React renames it for browsers to read

rubric: JSX is JavaScript, where `class` is reserved, so the DOM property name `className` is used.
Distractors invent CSS scoping or HTML deprecation reasons.

items.prompt: Which statements about React state are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: Writing `count++` on a state variable updates the screen reliably
State set in a child automatically changes the parent's state
Calling the setter function causes the component to re-render
Each rendered instance of a component keeps its own state

rubric: Setters trigger re-renders, and state is local to each component instance.
Direct mutation does not trigger rendering, and state does not propagate upward by itself.

items.prompt: A page renders `<Counter />` twice, side by side. Each has a button that runs `setCount(count + 1)` with `useState(0)`. A user clicks the first button three times. The first shows 3, and the second still shows 0. Why?

options.label: The second Counter must be re-mounted before it can read the shared count
Each Counter instance has its own independent state, so clicks affect only one
React keeps only one count and shows it in the first matching component
The second Counter is paused until it is clicked for the first time

rubric: State is created per component instance, so two Counters hold separate values.
Distractors imagine shared state or paused components.

items.prompt: Given `const [n, setN] = useState(0);` and a button with `onClick={() => { setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1); }}`, what does `n` show after one click?
rubric: Both calls use the same `n` from the current render (0), so both set 1.
Choosing 2 assumes the state updates between the two calls.

items.prompt: `names` is an array of unique strings. Which JSX correctly renders one `<li>` per name inside a `<ul>`?

options.label:
`{names.map(n =>
  • {n}
    • )}`

`{names.map(n =>
  • {n}
    • ).join('')}`

`{names.forEach(n =>
  • {n}
    • )}`

`{for (const n of names)
  • {n}
    • }`

rubric: `map` returns an array of elements that JSX can render.
`forEach` returns undefined, a `for` loop is a statement and not allowed in braces, and `join` creates a string.

items.prompt:
`function Greeting({ name }) { return

Hello, {name}

; }`. Which usage renders "Hello, Ana"?

options.label: `<Greeting props="Ana" />`
`<Greeting name="Ana" />`
`<Greeting {name="Ana"} />`
`<Greeting>Ana</Greeting>`

rubric: The destructured prop `name` must be passed as an attribute called `name`.
Children text goes to `children`, and the other forms use wrong syntax or the wrong prop name.

items.prompt:
You want to show `

Welcome

` only when the boolean `isLoggedIn` is true. Which JSX does this?

options.label:
`

Welcome

`

`{isLoggedIn &&

Welcome

}`

`{isLoggedIn}

Welcome

`

`{if (isLoggedIn)

Welcome

}`

rubric: `&&` inside braces is an expression that renders the element only when true.
`if` statements and an `if` attribute are not valid JSX, and the last option always shows the paragraph.

items.prompt: `todos` is state from `useState([])`. Which line correctly adds `newTodo` so the UI updates?

options.label: `setTodos(todos)` after pushing
`setTodos([...todos, newTodo])`
`todos.push(newTodo)`
`setTodos(todos.push(newTodo))`

rubric: Creating a new array and passing it to the setter lets React see a change.
Mutating the existing array, or passing it back, does not give React a new value.

items.prompt: Which of these attach a click handler correctly in JSX? Select all that apply.

options.label: `<button onClick={() => handleDelete(id)}>`
`<button onClick={handleClick}>`
`<button onClick={handleClick()}>`
`<button onclick="handleClick()">`

rubric: Pass a function reference, or an arrow function that calls the handler with an argument.
`handleClick()` runs during render, and the lowercase string form is HTML, not JSX.

items.prompt: A form has `const [name, setName] = useState('');` and renders `<input value={name} />`. The user types, but the text box never changes. You need the box to show what the user types.

options.label: Wrap the input in a `<form>` tag so the browser can store the typed text
Call `setName` once inside the component body so the input is unlocked
Replace `value` with `defaultValue` and keep calling `setName` in render
Add `onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}` so state follows each keystroke

rubric: A controlled input needs an onChange handler that updates the state it displays.
Other options either call setters during render, change to an uncontrolled input without handling, or rely on markup that doesn't help.

items.prompt: A component has `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`. Its click handler runs `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);`. What is `count` on the next render after one click?
rubric: Each call uses the same `count` value (0) from that render's closure, so all three queue the value 1.
Choosing 3 assumes updates accumulate as if state changed immediately.

items.prompt: State `n` starts at 0. One handler runs `setN(x => x + 1); setN(x => x + 1); setN(x => x * 3);`. What is `n` after the next render?
rubric: Updater functions run in order on the latest queued value: 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 6.
Answer 3 or 2 comes from dropping or misordering an updater.

items.prompt:
You render `todos.map(t =>
  • {t.text}
    • )`. Todos come from a database with unique `id`, can be reordered and deleted, and two todos may share the same text. Which `key` should you use?

options.label: `key={t.text}`
`key={Math.random()}`
`key={index}`
`key={t.id}`

rubric: A stable unique id lets React match items correctly across reorders and deletions.
Index breaks on reorder, text may duplicate, and random keys force remounts on every render.

items.prompt: State is `const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'Ana', age: 30 })`. Which call correctly sets age to 31 while keeping the name, following React's rules for state updates?

options.label: `user.age = 31; setUser(user)`
`setUser({ age: 31 })`
`setUser({ ...user, age: 31 })`
`setUser(user.age = 31)`

rubric: Spreading into a new object preserves other fields and gives React a new reference.
`setUser({ age: 31 })` drops name, since setters replace state rather than merge it.

items.prompt: A `Profile` component receives a `userId` prop and must call `loadUser(userId)` after render, and again whenever `userId` changes, but not on other re-renders. Which hook usage does this?

options.label: `useEffect(() => { loadUser(userId); }, [userId]);`
`useEffect(() => { loadUser(userId); }, [loadUser]);`
`useEffect(() => { loadUser(userId); }, []);`
`useEffect(() => { loadUser(userId); });`

rubric: The dependency array `[userId]` re-runs the effect only when `userId` changes.
An empty array runs once only, and no array runs after every render.

items.prompt: `items` is an array that may be empty. Which JSX expressions render nothing visible (no stray text) when `items` is `[]` and render `<List />` when it has elements? Select all that apply.

options.label: `{items.length > 0 && <List />}`
`{items.length ? <List /> : null}`
`{items.length || <List />}`
`{items.length && <List />}`

rubric: Both a boolean comparison and a ternary with null yield nothing when empty.
`items.length && <List />` renders the number 0 when empty; the `||` form renders List when empty.

items.prompt: A `ProductRow` child receives `item` and an `onSelect(id)` callback from its parent. When the row's button is clicked, the parent must be told which product id was chosen. Which `onClick` prop on the button does this correctly?

options.label: `onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}`
`onClick={onSelect}`
`onClick={onSelect(item.id)}`
`onClick={() => onSelect}`

rubric: Wrapping in an arrow function defers the call until click and passes the id.
`onSelect(item.id)` runs during render; `onSelect` alone passes the event; the last never calls it.

items.prompt: A form field is `<input value={name} />` where `name` comes from `useState('')`. Users report they cannot type anything. What is the cause?

options.label: It is controlled but has no `onChange` updating `name`, so the value never changes
`value` should be `defaultValue` for any input rendered by a component
State setters are asynchronous, so the first typed character is always lost
Inputs must be wrapped in a `<form>` element for React state to track typing

rubric: A controlled input shows only state; without onChange the state never changes, so the field appears frozen.
Using defaultValue would make it uncontrolled but is not the only fix; the other options misattribute the cause.

items.prompt: A timer component does `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);`. The display goes to 1 and stays there. Why?

options.label: The cleanup function runs after each tick and cancels the interval early
`setInterval` is throttled by React, so only the first tick triggers a render
`setCount` can't be called from inside a timer callback outside event handlers
The callback closes over `count` from the first render (0), so it always sets 1

rubric: With `[]` deps the effect runs once and the callback holds a stale `count`; `setCount(c => c + 1)` fixes it.
Cleanup only runs on unmount or dependency change, not after each tick.

items.prompt: Inside `Dashboard` you define `function Chart() { const [zoom, setZoom] = useState(1); ... }` and render `<Chart />`. Each time `Dashboard` re-renders, Chart's zoom resets to 1. What explains this?

options.label: Chart lacks a `key` prop, which is required for state to persist between renders
Child components always reset their state when their parent re-renders
Chart is a new function each render, so React sees a new type and remounts it
`useState` only keeps its value if the initial value is an object or array

rubric: A component defined inside another gets a new identity each render, so React unmounts and remounts it, discarding state.
Children keep state across parent renders when their type and position are stable.

items.prompt: A component builds `const options = { page, sort };` in its body, then runs `useEffect(() => { fetchData(options).then(setRows); }, [options]);`. The network is hit continuously. What is the root cause?

options.label: `options` is a new object every render, so the effect re-runs each time
`setRows` is missing from the dependency array, so React re-runs the effect after every state update
Objects cannot be listed as dependencies, so React re-runs the effect on every single render
`fetchData` returns a promise, and effects may not start asynchronous work without cleanup

rubric: Dependencies compare by reference; a fresh object each render triggers the effect, which sets state and renders again.
Objects can be dependencies, and setState functions are stable and need no listing.

items.prompt: `Editor` does `const [text, setText] = useState(props.initialText);`. The parent later passes a different `initialText` after loading a new document, but the editor still shows the old text. Why?

options.label: The parent must call `setText` directly, since props can't flow into children
`useState` uses its initial value only on first mount, so later prop changes are ignored
React blocks prop changes to a child whose state was already modified by the user
`props.initialText` is cached by the browser until the page reloads

rubric: The initial argument is read only on mount; passing a `key` per document or lifting state resets or syncs it.
Props do update; the state copy simply does not follow them.

items.prompt: A child is exported as `React.memo(Row)`, yet it still re-renders on every parent render. Which parent usages explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Passing `count={n}` where the number from state is unchanged
Passing `style={{ color: 'red' }}` as an inline object
Passing `onSave={() => save(id)}` without `useCallback`
Passing `label={item.name}` where the string is unchanged

rubric: Inline functions and object literals are new references each render, defeating memo's shallow comparison.
Unchanged primitives compare equal, so they don't cause re-renders.

items.prompt: A cart component runs `const addItem = () => { items.push({ id: 7, qty: 1 }); setItems(items); };`. After clicking the button the list on screen does not change, though a console log shows the array now has one more element. What best explains this?

options.label: React re-renders only when state values are primitives such as numbers or strings, so array state never triggers a render
`push` is asynchronous, so `setItems` runs before the new element exists and React stores the old array
`setItems` only accepts updater functions, so passing an array directly is silently ignored by React
The same array reference was passed after mutation, so React sees no change and skips the render

rubric: React compares state with Object.is; the mutated array keeps its identity, so the update is bailed out. Use `setItems([...items, newItem])`.
`push` is synchronous and setters accept plain values, including arrays.

items.prompt: A component runs `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);`. The counter rises to 1 and then stays at 1. What is the cause?

options.label: `setCount` is asynchronous, so each interval tick fires before the previous state update has completed
The cleanup function runs every second and cancels the interval before the next tick can fire
The callback closed over `count` from the first render, so it keeps setting 0 + 1
Effects with an empty dependency array run only once, so the interval is never actually started

rubric: The effect ran once, so its callback holds the `count` value from that render (a stale closure); `setCount(c => c + 1)` fixes it.
Distractors blame async state or cleanup timing, which misread when closures capture values.

items.prompt:
A list renders `items.map((t, i) =>
    • )`. After the first item is deleted, the remaining inputs show the wrong text. Why?

options.label: Index keys make React reuse DOM inputs by position, and `defaultValue` is only read on mount
Deleting from the array in state mutates it, so React cannot detect the change and re-render the list at all
React skips re-rendering list items whose index is unchanged, so the new item props are ignored by those rows
`defaultValue` is deprecated and stops updating after the first change to the array it was rendered from

rubric: Keys by index tie component and DOM identity to position, and `defaultValue` applies only at mount, so stale text stays.
Distractors invent skipped renders or mutation, which do not describe this keyed-reconciliation failure.

items.prompt: Inside `Form`, a developer writes `const Field = () => <input value={v} onChange={e => setV(e.target.value)} />;` and renders `<Field />`. The input loses focus after every keystroke. What is the cause?

options.label: `Field` is a new function each render, so React sees a new type and remounts the input
State set in a parent always blurs any child element, unless that element is given a ref to keep focus
The input is controlled, so React discards focus whenever its value prop changes between two renders
Typing triggers a full page reload because state changes inside a nested function component are not batched

rubric: A component defined inside another gets a new identity each render, so React unmounts and remounts it, losing focus.
Distractors blame controlled inputs or batching, which do not cause remounts.

items.prompt: A component has `const options = { page, size }; useEffect(() => { load(options).then(setData); }, [options]);`. The network tab shows endless requests. What is the cause?

options.label: Objects in a dependency array are compared by value, so changing `page` and `size` keeps retriggering the effect
An effect that calls an async function should have no dependency array, and listing one makes it loop
`options` is a new object each render, so its identity changes, the effect refires and `setData` re-renders
Calling `setData` inside a `then` callback is not allowed and forces React to re-run every effect on the page

rubric: Dependencies are compared with Object.is, so a fresh object each render refires the effect, whose state update causes another render.
Distractors claim value comparison or ban async effects, which are false.

items.prompt: `Row` is wrapped in `React.memo`, yet profiling shows it re-renders on every parent render. The parent renders `<Row item={item} onSelect={() => select(item.id)} />`. Why does the memo not help?

options.label: Reading `item` as an object prop disables memoization, because React cannot compare object props at all
The inline arrow is a new function each render, so the shallow prop comparison always finds a difference
Memoized components re-render whenever the parent's state changes, whatever the props passed down happen to be
`React.memo` works only on class components, so function components always re-render with their parent

rubric: React.memo does a shallow prop comparison; a new function reference each render fails it.
Distractors misstate what memo supports or how it compares props.

items.prompt: Which situations cause a component's local state to be reset? Select all that apply.

options.label: The parent renders a different component type at the same position
The parent re-renders and passes the same props
Its `key` prop changes between renders
A prop value changes while its key and type stay the same

rubric: A changed key or a changed type at the same position unmounts the old instance and mounts a fresh one.
Re-renders or prop changes alone preserve state, which the other options wrongly assume.

items.prompt: A search box runs `useEffect(() => { fetch('/api?q=' + query).then(r => r.json()).then(setResults); }, [query]);`. A user types "re" then quickly "react". Occasionally the list shows results for "re" even though the box says "react". What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The effect runs before the input value is committed, so it reads the previous query from the old render
The debounce is missing, which makes React batch both requests into one stale response for the older text
Responses can arrive out of order, and the effect has no cleanup to ignore results from a stale query
State updates from fetch callbacks are queued and always applied in reverse order of the requests made

rubric: Without a cleanup flag or abort, a slow earlier response can overwrite a newer one: a race condition.
Distractors invent batching or ordering rules that React does not have.

items.prompt: A `Toolbar` holds a filter input and a sibling `ProductList` must show filtered rows. Criteria: one source of truth, narrowest scope, no extra libraries. Which design is best?

options.label: Lift the filter state to their closest common parent and pass the value and setter down as props
Put the filter in a context at the app root so any component in the whole application can read it
Store the filter in a module-level variable and force both siblings to re-render whenever it is modified
Keep a copy of the filter in each sibling and sync the two copies using effects that run on every change

rubric: Lifting state to the nearest common parent gives a single source of truth at the narrowest scope.
Distractors duplicate state, use mutable globals, or widen scope beyond the criteria.

items.prompt: A list page has state `products` and `query`. Criteria: no sync bugs, minimal code. Which approach to the filtered list is best?

options.label: Store `filtered` in state and update it in the input handler together with `query`, so both change at once
Store `filtered` in a ref so it is updated without causing an extra render when the query changes
Store `filtered` in state and update it in an effect whenever `query` changes, to avoid recomputing each render
Keep only `products` and `query` in state and compute the filtered list during render

rubric: Derived values should be computed during render so they cannot drift from their sources.
Distractors duplicate derived data in state or refs, which creates sync bugs.

items.prompt: A light/dark theme changes a few times a month and is read by about 40 components at varied depths. Criteria: avoid threading props through intermediate components; re-render cost is acceptable. Which is best?

options.label: A mutable ref holding the theme, since refs notify every reading component automatically when they change value
A `useState` in each consumer initialised from `localStorage`, since this isolates updates to a single component each
Prop drilling through every layer, since explicit props guarantee that no component ever re-renders unnecessarily
A context provider near the root, since the value rarely changes so consumer re-renders are cheap

rubric: Context fits rarely-changing, widely-read values and avoids drilling; the re-render cost only matters for frequent updates.
Distractors ignore the stated criteria or misstate how refs and local state behave.

items.prompt: A teammate wraps every value and handler in `useMemo`/`useCallback` 'for performance', with no profiling. Criteria: readability, correctness, measured benefit. Which review comment is best?

options.label: Keep them all, since memoization is cheap and stale values are avoided once the dependencies are listed correctly
Remove most and re-add them where profiling shows a cost, since each adds overhead and dependency risk
Keep them on handlers only, since recreating functions on each render is the main cause of slow renders in React
Replace them with `React.memo` on every component, since its shallow prop comparison costs little and avoids most re-renders

rubric: Memoization has costs and stale-dependency risk, so apply it where measurement shows a benefit.
Distractors assume memoization is free or that functions are inherently expensive.

items.prompt: A small team's app fetches the same user and project data on many pages. Criteria: shared caching, request deduplication, stale-response handling, little code to maintain. Which approach is best?

options.label: Store every response in `localStorage` and read it on mount, since the browser handles invalidation for you
Adopt a data-fetching library with a cache, since dedupe, caching and stale responses are already handled
Fetch everything once in the root component and pass results down as props to avoid any duplicate requests
Hand-write `useEffect` fetches in each component, since this gives full control with the least amount of code

rubric: A caching data library meets all stated criteria with little code.
Distractors keep per-component effects or hand-rolled caches that the team would have to maintain and that miss dedupe or invalidation.

items.prompt: Which are sound reasons to prefer `useReducer` over several `useState` calls for a form's state? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is required whenever the state holds an object or an array rather than a primitive
The next state depends on the previous state and an action, and a pure reducer is easy to unit test
Several fields change together in one transition, so one reducer keeps every update consistent
It avoids re-rendering, because `dispatch` never triggers a render the way a state setter does

rubric: Reducers centralise related transitions and are pure, testable functions.
Dispatch does trigger renders, and objects work fine with useState.

items.prompt: A table renders 5,000 rows and typing in its filter box feels sluggish. Profiling shows most time goes to mounting and laying out thousands of DOM nodes. Criteria: keep a single scrolling list, minimal change to row code, measurable gain. Which fix is best?

options.label: Wrap each row in `React.memo`, which removes the cost of mounting and laying out all 5,000 DOM nodes
Replace `map` with a `for` loop that builds the array, since loops are much faster than `map` for large lists
Virtualize the list so only visible rows are rendered, which cuts the DOM node count at the source
Move the rows into context so React skips reconciling the list whenever the filter text changes on update

rubric: Virtualization addresses the profiled bottleneck, the DOM node count, while keeping one scrolling list.
Memo does not avoid mounting; context and loop rewrites do not reduce DOM size.

items.prompt: A search box filters a 10,000-row table. Typing lags because each keystroke re-renders every row. Criteria: the input must stay responsive, results must end up consistent with the query, and code changes must be minimal. Which approach best fits?

options.label: Wrap the parent's returned JSX in `useMemo` keyed on the query so the table is not rebuilt on keystrokes
Debounce the `setQuery` call by 300ms so the controlled input value and the table update less often
Give the table a new `key` on each keystroke so React discards the old rows quickly instead of diffing
Pass the query through `useDeferredValue` for the filter and wrap the row component in `React.memo`

rubric: Deferring the value keeps typing urgent and the heavy filter low priority, while memoised rows skip unchanged work.
Debouncing setQuery delays the input's own update, and useMemo on parent JSX doesn't stop the state-driven re-render.

items.prompt: A reviewer sees `const [full, setFull] = useState(''); useEffect(() => setFull(first + ' ' + last), [first, last]);`. Judging by correctness and simplicity, which critique is best?

options.label: Move the effect into a custom hook so the derived value can be reused in other components without duplicating the sync logic
Compute `first + ' ' + last` during render, since the effect adds an extra render and a stale frame
Switch the effect to `useLayoutEffect` so the update lands before the browser paints and the stale frame never shows
Add `setFull` to the dependency array so the effect always stays in sync with the latest state value it writes

rubric: Derived values should be calculated in render; syncing through an effect causes a second pass with an inconsistent intermediate output.
The other options keep the redundant state and only tweak when the sync happens.

items.prompt: A context provider holds `{x, y}` mouse coordinates updated on every mousemove, and 200 components consume it, most reading only `x`. Judge which critique and remedy best fit the stated goal of minimal re-rendering.

options.label: Switch the consumers to `React.memo`, because memo compares props and so also blocks re-renders triggered by context changes
Replace the context with props passed down from the root, since unchanged props never trigger re-renders of child components
Every consumer re-renders on any value change, so move the data to a store read with `useSyncExternalStore` selectors
Wrap the context value in `useMemo` keyed on `x` and `y`, so consumers skip re-rendering when the coordinates change

rubric: Context has no selector mechanism, so any change re-renders all consumers; a store with selectors limits updates to what is read.
useMemo can't help when the value really changes, and memo doesn't block context-triggered renders.

items.prompt: A sortable list renders rows with uncontrolled `<input>` fields and uses `key={index}`. After sorting, typed text stays at the same screen positions rather than moving with their records. Which judgement is best?

options.label: The inputs should be made controlled, because uncontrolled inputs can't survive any reorder
Index keys are fine here, but the sort should mutate the array in place to preserve identity
Wrap the rows in `React.memo` so they keep their typed values across the sort
Index keys tie component state to position, so use a stable record id as key

rubric: Keys identify items; with index keys React reuses the DOM and state by position, so state doesn't follow the record.
Memo and in-place mutation don't change how React matches elements to state.

items.prompt: A 40-field form validates only on submit, and profiling shows each keystroke re-rendering the whole form. Criteria: fewest re-renders, no new libraries, simple reading of values. Which approach is best?

options.label: Use uncontrolled inputs with names and read them via `FormData` on submit
Store each field in `useRef` and force updates with a counter after every keystroke
Keep all fields controlled in one state object and add `React.memo` to the form root
Lift every field into context so only the field that changed re-renders

rubric: With submit-only validation, uncontrolled inputs avoid per-keystroke renders and need no extra code.
Memo on the root doesn't help when its own state changes, and forced updates or context still re-render widely.

items.prompt: Review: `useEffect(() => { fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(setData); }, [url]);` where `url` changes as the user navigates. Which critiques are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: A slow earlier response can arrive after a newer one and overwrite its data
The effect should be `useLayoutEffect` to prevent a flash of old content
`data` must be added to the dependency array or the effect is stale
A failed request leaves old data shown with no error or loading signal

rubric: Without abort or ignore logic, out-of-order responses cause races, and failures are not handled.
`data` is not read in the effect, and layout timing does not address either problem.

items.prompt: A team wraps `Chart` in `React.memo` to cut renders when its parent updates every second. It still re-renders every time. The parent renders `<Chart options={{ smooth: true }} data={data} />` and `data` is unchanged. Which judgement about the fix is best?

options.label: Pass `data` through context, because memo skips renders only for components that receive no props from the parent
Memo is unreliable for components that take object props, so remove it and gate the work inside a `useEffect` instead
The inline object is new each render, so hoist it to a constant or wrap it in `useMemo`
Replace memo with `useCallback`, because that hook caches prop objects and keeps their references stable across renders

rubric: Memo uses shallow comparison, and a fresh object literal fails it; stabilising the reference fixes it.
useCallback caches functions, and memo works fine with stable props.

items.prompt: A `ProfileForm` holds draft text in its own `useState`. When the parent switches from user A to user B, the old draft stays visible. Constraints: no effect that syncs state, no lifting draft state, minimal code. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Wrap the form in `useMemo` keyed on `user.id` so a new instance is created
Store the draft in a `useRef` that is replaced when `user.id` changes
Render `<ProfileForm key={user.id} user={user} />` so the form remounts per user
Add `useEffect(() => setDraft(''), [user.id])` inside the form to clear the draft

rubric: Changing the key resets the component's state without effects or lifting state.
The effect violates the constraint, and refs and useMemo don't reset state identity.

items.prompt: Design `useWindowWidth()` for a concurrent-rendering app. It must never show two different widths in one render pass, must clean up its listener, and must work with a server-render fallback. Which design fits?

options.label: Keep the width in a `useRef` that a resize listener updates, and return `ref.current` from the hook during render
Use `useState(window.innerWidth)` and update it from a resize listener added in `useEffect`, removed in its cleanup
Call `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => window.innerWidth, () => 1024)` with a resize subscribe
Read `window.innerWidth` directly in render and force a re-render of the whole app from a timer every second

rubric: useSyncExternalStore prevents tearing, handles unsubscribe, and accepts a server snapshot.
useState with effect can tear or mismatch on the server, and refs don't trigger renders.

items.prompt: Design a like button with optimistic UI. Constraints: the server is the source of truth, rapid clicks must not desync the count, and a failed request must roll back only its own change. Which design fits?

options.label: Disable the button until the request returns, then set the count from the response
Increment the count in state immediately and decrement it again in the catch block of each request
Store the count in a `useRef` and call `forceUpdate` after each click and each failure
Keep confirmed count plus a list of pending changes; render the sum and drop a change when it settles

rubric: Deriving the display from confirmed data plus pending items makes concurrent rollbacks independent and the server authoritative.
Increment/decrement can desync under races, and disabling the button drops optimism and fast clicks.

items.prompt: Design `Tabs`, `Tab` and `Panel` as a compound component. Constraints: consumers may wrap `Tab` in their own components at any depth, no prop drilling, and no dependence on child element types. Which design satisfies them?

options.label: Require consumers to pass an `activeId` prop through every wrapper they create
Store the active id in a module-level variable that `Tab` and `Panel` both import
`Tabs` provides active id and setter via context, and `Tab` and `Panel` read it with a hook
`Tabs` maps over `children` and uses `cloneElement` to inject `active` into each child

rubric: Context reaches descendants at any depth and doesn't inspect child types.
cloneElement only reaches direct children, and module variables don't trigger renders.

items.prompt: Design state for a 5-step checkout wizard. Constraints: users can go back and edit earlier answers, an Undo must restore the previous full state, and updates must stay pure and testable. Which design fits?

options.label: One `useReducer` whose state holds `{present, past}`, with actions returning new snapshots
Separate `useState` per step plus a `useRef` array mutated on each change for undo
A single state object mutated in place, with a copy saved to `localStorage` on each step
Per-step components holding their own state, remounted via `key` to simulate undo

rubric: A reducer with history snapshots is pure, testable and makes Undo a single action.
Mutation and remounting lose or corrupt earlier state, and scattered state makes full restores hard.

items.prompt: A proposed search design calls `fetch` inside an effect on every keystroke. Requirements: no stale results, few requests, and cancelling on unmount. Which additions does the design still need? Select all that apply.

options.label: A new `key` on the input for every keystroke
The effect depending on the debounced query rather than the raw one
Wrapping the fetch call in `useCallback` with an empty array
A debounced copy of the query held in state
An `AbortController` aborted in the effect cleanup

rubric: Abort handles stale and unmounted requests; a debounced value, used as the dependency, cuts request count.
useCallback with an empty array risks stale closures, and changing the input key breaks typing.

items.prompt: A dashboard has 12 widgets that each call `fetch('/api/metrics')` on mount, producing 12 identical requests. Constraints: no new libraries, widgets stay independently placeable, and no request waterfall. Which design best meets them?

options.label: Save the response in `localStorage` and have widgets read it on mount
Wrap each widget's fetch in `useMemo` so duplicate calls are skipped
A shared cache keyed by URL that stores the in-flight promise, read by widgets through a hook
Fetch once in the root and pass the result to every widget as props through each layer

rubric: Caching the in-flight promise by key dedupes requests, parallelises loads and keeps widgets decoupled.
Root fetching forces prop drilling, and useMemo is per component, so it does not share across widgets.
